bib.title: Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Solving a Million-Step LLM Task with Zero Errors" (MAKER), Meyerson, Paolo, Dailey, Shahrzad, Francon, Hayes, Qiu, Hodjat, Miikkulainen (Cognizant AI Lab, UT Austin). arXiv 2511.09030v1, preprint, 12 Nov 2025.

COVERAGE: 29 of 29 pages, 93,377 characters. I read the body, the discussion and Appendices A to F in full. References were skimmed. In Appendix C I read the prompts and part of the parser code, not all of it. In Appendix D I read only the opening samples. In Appendix B I read the headings only.

CORE CLAIM: Cutting a task into single-step subtasks lets you vote on each step. Each agent sees only the current state and the strategy. The authors call this a massively decomposed agentic process (MDAP). With it, a small non-reasoning model solved a task of over one million dependent steps with no errors. Cost grows roughly as s·ln s when each agent gets one step. It grows exponentially in steps per agent.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. **Result.** 20-disk Towers of Hanoi (2^20 − 1 steps) was solved with zero errors using gpt-4.1-mini.
   - Setup: k_min = 3, first-to-ahead-by-k voting. Output cap 750 tokens, red-flag parser. Temperature 0 for the first vote, 0.1 afterwards. One run.
   - Quote: "With gpt-4.1-mini as the base model, the maximum output token threshold was set to 750, and a red-flagging output parser was used to enforce the basic formatting requirements. Beyond this cutoff, the model often found itself in confusing logical loops" (p10).
   - The paper reports no measured dollar total for the run. The only cost figure is a projection: about $3.5K for gpt-4.1-mini at τ=0.1 and about $4.9K at τ=1.0, both at t=0.95 (Fig 6b, p10). The table extraction is partly garbled, so verify against the PDF.
2. **Per-step error and model choice.** Small non-reasoning models match reasoning models on per-step error, and the rate stays flat as disks increase.
   - Setup: 10K random steps, no red-flagging, 2048-token cap, repairing parser.
   - Mean error rates: gpt-4.1-nano 0.3583, gpt-4.1-mini 0.0045, o3-mini 0.0017 (Fig 6a, p10).
   - Projected costs at t=0.95 include gpt-oss-20B $1.7K, deepseek-v3.1 $14.6K, haiku-4.5 $71.2K, gpt-4.1-nano $41.9K.
3. **Compounding, formula and scaling laws (theory, not measured).**
   - Quote: "a system with a 1% per-step error rate is expected to fail after only 100 steps of a million-step task" (p2).
   - p_full = (1 + ((1−p)/p)^k)^(−s/m), Eq 13.
   - k_min = Θ(ln s) (Eq 14).
   - Expected cost is Θ(s ln s) at m=1 (Eq 18) and Θ(p^−m · c · s · ln s) in general (Eq 17).
   - The derivation assumes errors are i.i.d. and that the correct answer races against a single most-likely alternative.
4. **Ablation: decomposition level m.** Figure 5 is theory only, from Eq 17.
   - Cost rises exponentially with steps per agent. Quote: "Notably, the cost grows exponentially with m" (p7).
   - The mechanism is that exact-match agreement across samples vanishes as an agent makes more decisions.
   - There is no empirical run at m>1 on Hanoi.
5. **Ablation: red-flagging.** Flagging means discarding responses that are too long or badly formatted.
   - Error rate jumps once responses pass about 700 tokens. It is still about 90% correct, but far worse than the roughly 1-in-1000 error rate on shorter responses (Fig 9a, p11).
   - The main benefit is fewer correlated errors. Counting steps where both of the first two votes were wrong ("collisions"), the discard parser had fewer than the repairing parser (Fig 9b, p12). Exact counts are not in the extraction.
   - Quote: "the impact on correlated errors turns out to be a much more important effect" (p11).
6. **Error decorrelation and convergence.**
   - Two independent runs of gpt-4.1-mini (τ=0.1) on the 10K sampled steps shared zero steps with errors in both (p10).
   - Undecided steps fell from 1,048,575 to 0 under first-to-ahead-by-3 (Fig 8, p11).
   - One pathological step (10241) took 18 voting rounds (Fig 8, App D).
   - First-to-k voting, which is weaker than first-to-ahead-by-k, also reached zero errors.
7. **Multiplication (preliminary).** A recursive version with decomposition and composition agents was tested on 5×5 and 6×6 digit multiplication with gpt-4.1-mini. The 5×5 solve rate reached 100% and the 6×6 rate reached 0.95 as k rose (App F, p28). The paper reports no other numbers for this.

LIMITS
- **Hanoi generalization.**
  - The strategy is given in every prompt. The authors state that this "isolates the ability of agents to execute clear instructions from the ability of LLMs to have insights" (p9). The paper tests execution, not planning.
  - Hanoi has a known optimal algorithm and a known correct answer at every step.
  - The decomposition is handed over. The authors say "it is assumed the definition of step is given a priori" and treat automatic discovery as open (p3).
  - Steps are uniform, with a stable p, which is why i.i.d. was reasonable. The authors say real tasks need different p per step and inexact matching of answers.
  - The multiplication test is only a preliminary sketch.
- The authors concede that correlated errors are "an open foundational problem". They concede that some tasks may resist decomposition. They also concede that a single step with an abnormally high error rate could sink a run.
- Only one 20-disk run is reported. The OpenAI API was chosen over together.ai for reliability.
- There is no comparison to code, tools, or a plain checkpointed loop. The authors waved that off as "not the point".
- Nothing here covers compaction versus context reset, session lifecycle, or external state files. Each agent is stateless and is handed the previous move and the full state. The state is the externalized artifact, and the agent must emit the next state.
- The safety and sentience arguments in the Discussion are speculative.

BUILDS ON
- Shojaee et al. 2025, "The Illusion of Thinking", arXiv 2506.06941 (Hanoi as a benchmark).
- Sinha et al. 2025, "The Illusion of Diminishing Returns", arXiv, on long-horizon execution (execution versus planning).
- Meyerson and Qiu, ICML 2025 position paper track, "Scaling LLM agents requires asymptotic analysis with LLM primitives" (AALPs, micro-roles).
- Sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) for first-to-ahead-by-k voting, and gambler's ruin (Wald, Feller; cited as refs [53–56]).
- Belcak et al. 2025, small language models for agentic AI, arXiv 2506.02153.
- Dziri et al. 2023 ("Faith and Fate", NeurIPS) on compounding error.

CODE: Appendix C, p18, holds the prompt template. Algorithms 1 to 3 on p4 give the voting loop. Algorithm 2 is the one worth keeping, with exact-match votes and the stop rule "if V[y] ≥ k + max_{v≠y} V[v]".

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 2, p4, "Core Components of MAKER". It shows pseudocode for decomposition, voting, and red-flagging. Figure 8, p11, "Convergence to zero-error solution", is the alternative. It shows undecided steps falling exponentially with the voting round.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions. Some equations and the Fig 6b table are garbled in the extraction, though the numbers I quote are legible. Reference [11] shows a malformed arXiv ID (2110.09624), which is probably an error in the paper itself.

FIT: Partially on-topic for 06-long-horizon-execution. It supports the per-step error compounding and decomposition sections strongly, with the math and a real run. It does not support the compaction versus reset section. For that, a note on fresh context per step could cite it only as the extreme case of stateless agents. For voting and redundancy as verification, 05-verification-loops.md or 07-orchestration.md may fit as well. The note is at /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/ai-engineering/03-harness-engineering/notes/06-long-horizon-execution.md.
